notes.h: How to write a fabric profile
notes.b: A profile follows one named fabric from its fibre to its end use, with the evidence used to identify it. Examiners ask for it under set headings, so knowing the structure lets you collect marks heading by heading.
points: Name the fabric and its fibres first, for example woven cotton or knitted polyester, because older marking schemes gave a mark for the name alone.
Fibre production: how the fibre is obtained from its raw material, or made from a polymer (a long chain of repeating units).
Yarn production: how the fibres become a yarn, either by spinning staple fibres (short fibres) or by twisting filaments (continuous fibres).
A yarn is fibres or filaments twisted together, and a fabric is made by weaving or knitting yarns, so keep these three terms apart.
Properties: give two or three properties, each linked to the fibre structure or the yarn, so the property has a reason behind it.
Identification: give the burning test result and the microscopic appearance of the fibres.
Uses: give suitable household or clothing uses, each with a reason based on the properties.
Other headings seen in past questions are fabric construction technique and fibre composition, so answer exactly the headings the question lists.
notes.tip: Answer under the headings the question gives and name the fabric first. Keep production, properties and tests for your named fabric only, rather than drifting into fibre classification or finishes.

notes.h: Natural fabric profile: cotton, from boll to yarn
notes.b: Cotton is the usual natural fabric to profile. Its production is a sequence of stages, and each stage has its own job, so learn them in order.
points: 1. Harvest: the bolls (seed pods) on the cotton plant open when the plant matures, and the fibres are picked by hand or machine.
2. Ginning: machines separate the fibres from the seeds and remove large impurities, so that only clean fibre goes on to be made into yarn.
3. Baling and grading: the fibres are baled and graded by length, fineness and colour, so that similar fibres are used together.
4. Cleaning and blending: fibres are cleaned and opened, and mixed so that the yarn is uniform.
5. Carding: fibres are combed into a loose web and drawn into a continuous sliver (a loose rope of fibres).
6. Combing (optional): combing before spinning removes short fibres, which gives a finer, smoother yarn.
7. Spinning: the sliver is twisted into yarn, because the twist is what holds the short fibres together.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the stages: ginning separates fibres from seeds, carding straightens fibres, combing removes short fibres and spinning twists them into yarn.

notes.h: Natural fabric profile: cotton properties, tests and uses
notes.b: Cotton's properties come from its fibre structure, and the same structure shows up in the burning test and under the microscope.
points: Properties: cotton is absorbent, strong and stronger when wet, cool and comfortable to wear, washable and dyes well, which is why it suits everyday clothing and household textiles.
Weaknesses: cotton creases easily unless treated, so it often needs ironing; it also shrinks, burns easily, may mildew and has little elasticity.
Burning test: cotton burns quickly with a steady yellow flame, keeps burning when removed from the flame, smells of burning paper and leaves a soft grey ash.
Microscope: each fibre is a flat, twisted ribbon with natural twists (convolutions), and a central canal (lumen) is visible.
Uses: shirts, jeans, towels, bed linen, curtains and T-shirts, where absorbency and washability matter.
notes.tip: In a burning test answer, give what the fibre does as it approaches the flame, in the flame and when removed, then the smell and the ash. Use the plain words examiners expect rather than inventing extra detail.

notes.h: Other natural fabrics examiners accept: wool, linen and silk
notes.b: A profile of any natural fabric is accepted, so you can write about wool, linen or silk instead of cotton. Each needs only a few points under each heading.
points: Wool production: shearing (clipping the fleece from the sheep), grading, scouring (washing out grease and dirt), carding and spinning.
Wool properties: warm, resilient and absorbent, but it shrinks and felts, so it needs careful washing.
Wool burning test: burns slowly with a smell of burnt hair or feathers and leaves a black, crushable ash.
Linen production: it comes from the flax stem, which is retted, scutched, combed and spun.
Linen properties and test: strong, absorbent and creases easily, so it often needs ironing; it burns quickly with a paper smell, like cotton.
Silk production: it comes from the cocoon, with the continuous filaments reeled off.
Silk properties and test: smooth, so it drapes well; it burns slowly with a burnt-hair smell and leaves a crushable black bead.
notes.tip: Pick one fabric and stay with it. Cotton, wool, linen and silk are all accepted for a natural fabric profile.

notes.h: Manufactured fabric profile: nylon, from polymer to yarn
notes.b: Manufactured fibres are made from chemicals rather than harvested. Nylon is the usual example, and its production turns small molecules into a long chain, then into filaments.
points: 1. Polymer: two chemicals (monomers), joined in equal proportions and heated, link up to form a long nylon polymer.
2. Extrusion: the molten polymer is forced through a spinneret, a plate with many fine holes, to form filaments.
3. Cooling: the filaments solidify and harden as they cool.
4. Drawing: the filaments are stretched to line up their molecules, which increases their strength.
5. Winding: the filaments are wound on bobbins, ready to be made into yarn.
Yarn production: the continuous filaments are twisted together into a filament yarn, which can be textured to add bulk.
notes.tip: Describe the monomers as two chemicals joined into a long polymer. Do not give a single pair of named chemicals as the only description of how nylon is made.

notes.h: Manufactured fabric profile: nylon properties, tests and uses
notes.b: Nylon's long, aligned molecules and smooth, non-absorbent filaments explain both its properties and what it does in a flame.
points: Properties: nylon is very strong, elastic, light, abrasion resistant (it resists rubbing and wear), low in absorbency and quick drying, and it resists creasing.
Weaknesses: nylon builds up static, may feel hot to wear because it absorbs so little moisture, and is flammable, melting when it burns.
Burning test: nylon melts and shrinks away from the flame, forms a hard bead and gives off a chemical smell.
Microscope: nylon appears as smooth, even, round rod-like filaments with no scales or twists.
Uses: hosiery, swimwear, lingerie, jackets and carpets, such as in tights and swimsuits, where strength, stretch and quick drying matter.
notes.tip: Give nylon's burning result in the scheme words: it melts and shrinks away from the flame, forms a hard bead and gives off a chemical smell, without inventing extra detail.

notes.h: Other manufactured fabrics examiners accept: polyester and viscose
notes.b: Polyester and viscose are also accepted as the manufactured fabric in a profile, and they are made in different ways.
points: Polyester production: a viscous liquid is extruded through a spinneret and solidifies in cold air.
Polyester properties: strong, crease resistant and non-absorbent, so it dries quickly.
Polyester burning test: it burns and melts, with a sweetish smell, and leaves a hard bead.
Viscose production: cellulose is treated and dissolved, then forced through a spinneret into a bath.
Viscose properties and test: it is weak when wet, so it needs gentle handling, and it burns like cotton because both are cellulose.
notes.tip: Say that nylon and polyester filaments are smooth and round. Do not claim a round cross-section for every manufactured fibre.

notes.h: Blended fabric profile: polyester and cotton (Higher Level only)
notes.b: A blend combines two or more fibres in one yarn, or different yarns in the warp and weft, to get the best properties of each. This is different from joining two separate fabrics, because the fibres are combined in the yarn or in warp and weft.
points: Examples of blends are polyester-cotton, wool-nylon, cotton-Lycra and linen-cotton.
Production: each fibre is produced separately, with cotton harvested, ginned and cleaned and polyester extruded and cut into staple (short) lengths.
Yarn production: the staple fibres are blended before or during carding, then drawn and spun into one yarn.
A blend can also be made by using one fibre yarn for the warp and another for the weft.
Properties: cotton gives absorbency and comfort, while polyester gives strength, crease resistance and quick drying.
Compared with pure cotton, the blend dries faster, is easier to iron and is cheaper; in the same way, linen-cotton is cheaper than pure linen.
Burning test: the results are mixed, because the blend burns like cotton and melts like polyester, so the test is indicative only.
Microscope: both fibre types are visible in the same sample, with cotton's twisted ribbon beside polyester's smooth filaments.
Uses: shirts, school uniforms, bed linen and curtains, because easy care and comfort both matter there.
notes.tip: A blended fabric question asks for fibre production of both fibres, how they are blended, the properties of both and uses. Never give a single burning result for a blend: say the result is mixed and indicative only.

notes.h: Yarn and filament modification (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Modification changes a yarn or filament to improve the properties of the fabric made from it. Filament modification changes a continuous filament yarn so that it is bulkier, softer or stretchier, without changing the polymer. Examiners ask for two examples, so know several and what each achieves.
points: Modification examples in marking schemes include blending, crimping, twisting, mercerising, brushing, flame or stain resistance and water repellence.
Crimping and texturising: the filaments are crimped, looped or curled, trapping air so the yarn is bulkier, warmer and softer, as in textured (bulked) polyester.
Air-jet texturing: compressed air loops the filaments, giving bulk without mechanical crimping.
Heat setting: a textured yarn is heated under tension so that it keeps its crimp or loops in the finished fabric.
Twisting: more twist gives a stronger, smoother yarn, and ply yarns are made by twisting yarns together.
Mercerising: cotton under tension is treated with caustic soda, which gives extra lustre, strength, absorbency and a better affinity for dye.
Brushing raises the surface of the fabric, trapping air and giving a warmer, softer fabric.
Textured or slub yarns have uneven thick and thin sections, or loops added to the yarn, to create surface interest in a fabric.
notes.tip: Mercerising treats cotton yarn or fabric, but the marking scheme lists it under filament modification, so give it as one of your examples. Filament modification changes the filament yarn, not the polymer.

notes.h: Investigation: identifying a fibre by burning and microscope
notes.b: Fibre identification is an investigation in which a known control sample is compared with an unknown sample. Two tests are used together because one alone can mislead.
points: Aim: to identify an unknown fabric sample from its burning behaviour and its microscopic appearance.
Burning method: hold a small fibre sample with tongs or forceps, remove any finish where possible, and bring it slowly towards a flame held over a non-flammable surface.
Observations: record how the fibre behaves as it approaches the flame, as it burns and when removed from the flame, whether it melts, the smell and the appearance of the ash or residue.
Control: so the unknown has something to match, test a known sample of cotton, wool or nylon under the same conditions, and compare the results, so the unknown has something to be matched against.
Microscope: mount a few fibres on a slide, in water, examine them under magnification and compare their shape (twist, scales, rod or ribbon) with reference images.
Safety: ventilate the room, keep water and a fire blanket nearby, use small samples, tie back hair and do not breathe in fumes from the burning sample.
Limits: finishes and dyes change the results, and blends give mixed results, so use both tests together.
Conclusion: the fibre is identified when both the burning result and the microscopic appearance match a known fibre.
notes.tip: A burning test question asks you to explain the test with one example. Give the method, what you observe and the result for one fibre, such as cotton, and note that smell descriptions are subjective, so use the scheme words.

keyTerms.definition: A short fibre, such as cotton or wool, that must be spun together with other fibres to make a yarn.
A continuous, very long fibre, such as silk or a man-made fibre, that can be twisted into a yarn without spinning.
The process of separating cotton fibres from their seeds and removing large impurities.
The process of combing fibres into a loose, aligned web and drawing them into a sliver.
A treatment of cotton with caustic soda under tension, which increases its lustre, strength and affinity for dye.
A process that crimps or loops filaments to add bulk, softness and warmth to a yarn.
A method of identifying a fibre by observing how it burns, whether it melts, its smell and the residue it leaves.
A method of identifying a fibre by its shape, surface and cross-section when viewed under magnification.
A yarn made from two or more different fibres mixed together to combine their properties.

factCards.term: Two methods of identifying a fibre
factCards.definition: The burning test and microscopic evaluation.

factCards.term: Four stages of cotton fibre production
factCards.definition: Harvesting the bolls, ginning, cleaning and blending, and carding.

factCards.term: Three stages in making nylon filament
factCards.definition: The polymer is formed from monomers, extruded through a spinneret, and cooled and drawn into filament.
It burns readily with a steady flame, smells of burning paper, keeps burning when removed and leaves soft grey ash.
It burns slowly, self-extinguishes, smells of burning hair and leaves a crushable black bead.
A flat, twisted ribbon with natural convolutions and a central canal (lumen).
Overlapping scales on the surface of each fibre.

factCards.term: Two ways filament yarn is textured
factCards.definition: Crimping (or false-twist texturising) and air-jet texturing.

questions.prompt: Describe how a burning test could show whether an unknown sample is wool or nylon.
questions.model: Remove any finish, hold a small sample with forceps and bring it slowly to a flame over a non-flammable surface. Wool burns slowly, shrinks and curls away, tends to self-extinguish when removed, smells of burning hair and leaves a crushable black bead. Nylon melts and shrinks away from the flame, forms a hard bead and gives off a chemical smell. Compare the results with a known wool and a known nylon control, and ventilate the room with water and a fire blanket nearby.

questions.prompt: Prepare a profile of one fabric made from a manufactured fibre. Cover how the fibre is produced, how the yarn is made, two properties of the fabric, the identification results and a suitable use.
questions.model: Fibre production: a polymer is formed by heating monomers together; the molten polymer is extruded through a spinneret, cooled and drawn into filaments. Yarn production: the continuous filaments are twisted into a filament yarn, which can be textured to add bulk and warmth. Properties: polyester is strong, crease resistant, quick drying and low in absorbency; nylon is strong, elastic and abrasion resistant. Identification: in a burning test the sample melts and shrinks away from the flame and forms a hard bead; under the microscope the filaments are smooth, uniform and round in cross-section with no scales or convolutions. Use: a polyester shirt or fleece, chosen because it resists creasing and dries quickly, or a nylon carpet, chosen because it is hard wearing.
